candidate.answerReason: The shared digit must be at least \(23-(9+8)=6\) and at most \(12-(1+2+3)=6\). It is therefore 6, and the six-digit total is \(23+12-6=29\).

methods.label: Bound the shared digit
methods.explanation:
The figure has three squares in the column and four in the row, with one square shared. Adding the two given sums counts that shared digit twice, so finding it will let us find the total.

Let \(x\) be the shared digit. The other two digits in the column are different digits from 1 through 9, so their sum is at most \(9+8=17\). To make the column sum 23, we must have
\[
x\ge 23-17=6.
\]
The other three digits in the row are also different, so their sum is at least \(1+2+3=6\). To make the row sum 12, we must have
\[
x\le 12-6=6.
\]
Together these bounds force \(x=6\). This is possible: use 8 and 9 in the other column squares and 1, 2, and 3 in the other row squares. These six digits are all different and give the required sums.

In \(23+12\), every digit is counted once except the shared 6, which is counted twice. Subtracting its extra copy gives
\[
23+12-6=\boxed{29},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The bounds come directly from the largest two and smallest three distinct allowed digits. The reasoning requires only elementary comparisons and addition and subtraction.
